title: Thermodynamic theory of voting and EU elections
authors: Klaus M. Frahm, Dima L. Shepelyansky
abstract: We introduce a thermodynamic theory of voting and show that it provides a good description of distribution of party votes in EU elections. The theory traces parallels between system energies of coupled nonlinear oscillators and party vote fractions. Such a classical system evolution is characterized by the conservation of total energy and probability norm that leads to the Rayleigh-Jeans (RJ) thermalization and condensation at low energy states. A similar thermalization also describes the wealth inequality in society. This feature belongs to the phenomena of constraint driven condensation known in statistical mechanics. We show that the RJ theory well depicts the Lorenz and Pareto curves obtained from the EU vote results. The theory also recovers the dispersion of votes between candidates of first round presidential elections in France.
summary: This paper proposes a Thermodynamic Theory of Voting (TTV) that models political vote distribution using principles from statistical mechanics. It shows that the observed inequality in election results closely follows patterns predicted by Rayleigh-Jeans thermalization and condensation phenomena. This suggests that electoral outcomes can be analyzed using tools developed for studying wealth or energy distributions in physical systems.
main_problem: To develop a Thermodynamic Theory of Voting (TTV) that statistically describes the distribution of party votes in large-scale elections, drawing parallels with established physical models.
main_result: The TTV successfully provides a good statistical description for vote distributions in EU and French elections by modeling them using Rayleigh-Jeans (RJ) thermalization and condensation phenomena.
method: The authors adapt concepts from statistical mechanics, particularly the Wealth Thermalization Hypothesis, to model political interactions as an energy conservation system governed by RJ statistics.
model_or_system: The system models party votes/political power distribution using coupled nonlinear oscillators whose energies are analogous to vote fractions. The theory relies on deriving distributions from conserved total energy and probability norm.
key_observables: Lorenz curves, Pareto curves, and the Gini coefficient ($G$) are used as primary diagnostics to quantify inequality in vote shares.
important_parameters: Temperature/Energy ($\epsilon$), number of parties ($N_p$), and model parameters derived from fitting real data (e.g., $a$ parameter for RJE).
main_assumptions: The theory assumes that opinion formation results from complex, classical nonlinear interactions leading to thermalization; the analysis is based on the RJ distribution.
figures_summary: Figures compare empirical Lorenz and Pareto curves from EU/French elections (2014-2024) against theoretical predictions derived from the RJS model. Maps show Gini coefficients across various EU countries.
paper_structure: The paper introduces TTV, establishes parallels with wealth inequality models exhibiting RJ condensation, details the use of Lorenz/Pareto curves and Gini coefficients, and applies these methods systematically to multiple historical election datasets (EU and French).
why_interesting: While not directly quantum, the core mathematical machinery—thermalization, energy conservation, and phase transitions leading to condensation—is central to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, which informs open quantum systems dynamics.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
